rows.question: What does Chapter 3 say about sovereign debt in developing economies?
rows.expected: Chapter 3 finds that rising government debt in EMDEs leads to higher interest rates, higher debt-service payments and a greater likelihood of debt distress. Debt levels are positively and non-linearly associated with dollar-denominated sovereign spreads and domestic-currency bond yields; the rise in EMDE debt-to-GDP since 2010 is associated with increases of about 110 basis points in spreads and 30 basis points in yields. Rising advanced-economy debt adds to the pressure, and effects are larger in countries with a history of default, low credit ratings, frontier-market status, reliance on short-term debt and weak governance. EMDE government debt rose from under 40 percent of GDP in 2010 to over 70 percent. It recommends stronger revenue mobilization, more efficient spending, better debt management, domestic debt market development and, where appropriate, debt-for-development swaps.

This rise in debt levels is positively associated with dollar-denominated sovereign bond spreads and domestic-currency government bond yields in a non-linear manner [^2]. Consequently, the cost of servicing government debt has risen from 6 percent of government revenues in 2010 to an estimated 11 percent in 2025 [^3].
